title: Module 2 · Lesson 2 — Structured output and constrained decoding

lines: Lesson two is structured output and constrained decoding.
Agents need values that always parse, not prose that usually does.
Picture an expense bot that files receipts into a finance system.
That system accepts exactly twelve categories, and nothing else.
Now and then, the bot invents a thirteenth category, like team vibes.
The import rejects it, and the whole batch fails.
Asking for JSON in the prompt guarantees nothing.
Validating and retrying usually works eventually, but costs extra round trips and can still fail.
Provider JSON or schema mode is the common production default.
It returns valid JSON matching your schema, at no extra cost.
Constrained decoding goes further: at every step, it masks out any token that would break the grammar.
Invalid output becomes impossible, not just unlikely.
NVIDIA's stack supports this as guided decoding in TensorRT-LLM and NIM, with backends like XGrammar and Outlines.
With an enum of the twelve categories, a thirteenth can never appear.

say.0: Nvidia's stack supports this as guided decoding in TensorRT-LLM and NIM, with backends like XGrammar and Outlines.
say.1: With an eenum of the twelve categories, a thirteenth can never appear.

lines: Next, schema-first development: define the output once, for example as a Pydantic model.
That one definition produces the schema for the model, validates what comes back, and types everything downstream.
Make escalation a field the model fills in, like requires human review.
A true or false beats string-matching prose.
Field order matters too: put the rationale before the verdict.
Then the model reasons first and decides second, instead of justifying a choice it already made.
Use enums for anything you'll branch on, and include an explicit unsure option, or the schema forces a confident guess.
And keep schemas shallow, because deep nesting raises the error rate.

say.0: Use eenums for anything you'll branch on, and include an explicit unsure option, or the schema forces a confident guess.

lines: Remember, structured output constrains form, not truth.
A perfectly valid record can still file a taxi ride as catering, so correctness needs grounding and evaluation.
A classic exam question: an agent must pick one of fifty tool names, and sometimes invents one.
Retries, lower temperature, and better prompts only reduce that; constrained decoding over an enum eliminates it.

say.1: Retries, lower temperature, and better prompts only reduce that; constrained decoding over an eenum eliminates it.

lines: Unlikely versus impossible is the distinction to remember.
